<p>
        Today's harness console embeds the same UI for every harness — git-graph, branches, code-server, etc. — even when those don't apply (a marketing harness has no code branches). The fix: <strong>each harness install registers its own UI</strong>.
      </p>

      

### 8.1 Reference apps studied



      <table>
        <thead><tr><th>App</th><th>Plugin model</th><th>Sandboxing</th><th>Distribution</th></tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td><strong>VS Code</strong></td><td>Manifest-declared contribution points (~30 surfaces)</td><td>Out-of-process extension host + iframe webviews</td><td>Runtime, ~50,000 extensions</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Backstage</strong></td><td>React packages registered at app build via DI container with typed services (`ApiRef`)</td><td>None</td><td>Build-time only</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Figma</strong></td><td>Plugin JS sandboxed; UI iframe with manifest-declared network allowlist</td><td>Strongest of all surveyed</td><td>Runtime marketplace</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>JupyterLab</strong></td><td>Lumino DI with typed tokens; whole app is plugins</td><td>None</td><td>Build OR runtime</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>WordPress (Gutenberg)</strong></td><td>Blocks via `registerBlockType()` + hooks system</td><td>None</td><td>Runtime, ~60,000 plugins</td></tr>
          <tr><td><strong>Obsidian</strong></td><td>Full DOM/Node access</td><td>None (cautionary tale — adding capability prompts post-incidents)</td><td>Runtime</td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

      

### 8.2 Papercusp UI plugin model — the hybrid



      <p>
        <strong>Backstage's API patterns + Figma's iframe sandbox + WordPress's hooks system.</strong>
      </p>

      <p><strong>Phase v1</strong> (next 1-2 months): plugins are React packages registered via DI container at build time. Reference plugins (papercup, sheets) ship with the runtime. No sandbox — too early for marketplace concerns.</p>

      <p><strong>Phase v2</strong> (when marketplace ships): same plugin manifest, but plugins ship as JS bundles loaded into iframe sandboxes. The DI container exposes services via postMessage RPC. Capabilities (§10) enforce at the iframe boundary.</p>

      

### 8.3 Plugin manifest (UI portion)



      

```
// packages/plugin-sdk/src/index.ts (extended) — the live interface is `Plugin`
export interface PapercuspPlugin {
  name: string;
  version: string;
  description: string;
  capabilities: Capability[];   // see §10

  // ── UI contribution ─────────────────────────────────
  ui?: {
    /** URL slug — mounted at /harness/<slug> */
    slug: string;
    /** Display name in the harness picker */
    label: string;
    /** Optional icon (lucide-react name or URL) */
    icon?: string;
    /** Lazy-loaded React component (Phase v1) */
    component: () => Promise<{ default: ComponentType<HarnessUIProps> }>;
    /** Optional sub-routes within /harness/<slug>/<sub> */
    subRoutes?: SubRouteContribution[];
  };

  // (Other axes from §7…)
}

/** Props the host passes to the plugin's UI component */
export interface HarnessUIProps {
  /** Slug of the harness install */
  slug: string;
  /** DI container — plugin reads its capability-scoped services via this */
  api: PapercuspApi;
  /** Read-only? (e.g., on the public site) */
  readOnly: boolean;
}
```



      

### 8.3.1 Manifest authoring — TS source, frozen JSON output



      <p>
        <em>Implemented (current state):</em> the manifest is authored
        directly as <code>papercusp.json</code> (validated against
        <code>papercusp-plugin.schema.json</code> with
        <code>additionalProperties: false</code>); the runtime entry point is a
        <code>Plugin</code> literal in <code>index.cjs</code> that asserts
        <code>satisfies Plugin</code>, so component/handler references are
        type-checked there. The <code>defineManifest()</code> /
        <code>papercusp build</code> / <code>jsonOnly</code> TS-source flow
        described below did not ship — it is preserved here as design
        rationale. See the
        <a href="/internal/docs/spec/plugin-quickstart">authoring quickstart</a>
        for the live manifest shape.
      </p>

      <p>
        The manifest is authored as TypeScript, not JSON. Component refs are
        type-checked at build time, eliminating the "componentId typo →
        runtime not-found" failure mode that plagues string-keyed manifest systems.
      </p>

      ```typescript
// papercusp.manifest.ts (authored)
import { defineManifest } from '@papercusp/plugin-sdk';
import WeatherTab from './components/WeatherTab';
import WeatherDashboard from './components/WeatherDashboard';

export default defineManifest({
  name: 'sample-weather',
  version: '0.1.0',
  capabilities: ['ui:dashboard-tab', 'http:fetch:api.weather.gov'],
  ui: {
    slug: 'sample-weather',
    label: 'Weather',
    component: WeatherDashboard,        // typed reference, not a string
  },
  dashboardTabs: [
    { id: 'weather', label: 'Weather', component: WeatherTab },
  ],
});
```

      <p>
        At publish time, `papercusp build` produces a frozen
        `papercusp.json` that lists components by stable componentId
        (e.g. `"./components/WeatherTab.js#default"`) for tools that
        don't have a TS runtime — the marketplace site, the install consent
        prompt, the registry. The JSON is generated, never hand-edited.
      </p>

      <p>
        Plugin authors who want to ship a JSON-only manifest may opt out via
        `defineManifest({ ...config, jsonOnly: true })` and accept
        the runtime-error tradeoff. Reference plugins (papercup, sheets,
        shareholder-briefings) all ship the TS form.
      </p>

      

### 8.4 The DI container (host services)



      <p>
        Plugins consume host state via typed services. The
        <code>PapercuspApi</code> exposes each service as a direct property
        (<code>api.tasks</code>, <code>api.goals</code>,
        <code>api.pendingEvents</code>, <code>api.routines</code>,
        <code>api.comments</code>, <code>api.secrets</code>,
        <code>api.storage</code>, <code>api.db</code>, <code>api.fetch</code>,
        <code>api.capabilities</code>); each call is a capability-gated proxy
        that throws <code>MissingCapabilityError</code> when the plugin's
        manifest hasn't declared the matching capability:
      </p>

      

```
// What plugins use — services are direct properties, not a useService() lookup:
const completedTasks = await api.tasks.list({ status: 'passed' });  // throws unless 'tasks:read' granted

// Service definitions live in @papercusp/plugin-loader (api-factory.ts),
// not the SDK; the SDK only exports the `defineService` helper + TS interfaces:
export const TasksServiceDef = defineService({
  name: 'tasks',
  methods: {
    list:      { capability: 'tasks:read' },
    get:       { capability: 'tasks:read' },
    lineage:   { capability: 'tasks:read' },
    create:    { capability: 'tasks:write' },
    setStatus: { capability: 'tasks:write' },
  },
});

export const RoutinesServiceDef = defineService({
  name: 'routines',
  methods: {
    list:    { capability: 'routines:read' },
    upsert:  { capability: 'routines:write' },
    delete:  { capability: 'routines:write' },
    trigger: { capability: 'routines:write' },  // manually fire — inserts a pending_event
  },
});

export const SecretsServiceDef = defineService({
  name: 'secrets',
  methods: {
    // resource-specific cap: 'secrets:read:YOUTUBE_API_KEY'
    read: { capability: (name) => 'secrets:read:' + name },
  },
});
```



      

### 8.4.1 Service ABI versioning



      <p>
        Service definitions evolve. Without a version contract, every substrate
        release risks silently breaking installed plugins. The substrate pins
        services by semver range in the plugin manifest:
      </p>

      ```typescript
// In the plugin manifest:
export default defineManifest({
  // ...
  services: {
    tasks:   '^1.0',
    secrets: '^2.0',
    routines: '^1.2',
  },
});
```

      <p>
        On load, the substrate compares the plugin's declared range against
        each service's runtime version. If the range doesn't satisfy, the
        plugin is rejected at install time — never silently downgraded.
      </p>

      <p><strong>Evolution rules</strong> (substrate maintainers must follow):</p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Patch</strong> (1.0.0 → 1.0.1): bug fixes only, no shape change.</li>
        <li><strong>Minor</strong> (1.0.x → 1.1.0): additive only — see "What counts as additive" below.</li>
        <li><strong>Major</strong> (1.x → 2.0): anything not on the additive list. Triggers a re-install consent prompt for every plugin pinning the old range.</li>
      </ul>

      <p><strong>What counts as additive</strong> (allowed in a minor bump):</p>

      <ul>
        <li>Adding a new method to the service.</li>
        <li>Adding a new <strong>optional</strong> parameter to an existing method (with a defined default).</li>
        <li>Adding a new <strong>optional</strong> field to a return-type schema.</li>
        <li>Widening a return-type union (`'a' | 'b'` → `'a' | 'b' | 'c'`) — but plugins should still treat unknown values as a degraded case.</li>
        <li>Narrowing an input-type union to be <em>more</em> permissive (accept additional input shapes the plugin can pass).</li>
      </ul>

      <p><strong>What does NOT count as additive</strong> (requires a major bump):</p>

      <ul>
        <li>Adding a <em>required</em> parameter, even with a TypeScript default — JSON callers don't see TS defaults and break.</li>
        <li>Removing or renaming any method, parameter, or return field.</li>
        <li>Narrowing a return-type union (removing a possible value).</li>
        <li>Narrowing an input-type union to be more restrictive (rejecting inputs that previously worked).</li>
        <li>Changing the meaning of an existing field (same name, different semantics).</li>
        <li>Tightening validation (e.g., a string field that previously accepted any value now requires a regex match).</li>
      </ul>

      <p>
        Authors who can't tell which side a change falls on should treat it as
        major. The cost of an over-cautious major bump is a re-prompt; the cost
        of a too-loose minor bump is silently broken installs.
      </p>

      <p>
        Service schemas are validated with Zod (or compatible) on every method
        return. A plugin compiled against v1.3 calling a v1.4 substrate gets
        the new optional fields silently dropped at the schema boundary — never
        a malformed object.
      </p>

      <p>
        This is the single highest-leverage rule for the marketplace's
        long-term health. Without it, "this plugin worked yesterday" becomes
        the most common bug class.
      </p>

      

### 8.5 The hooks system (WordPress-inspired)



      <p>
        <em>Implemented (current state):</em> the WordPress-style
        <code>PluginHookBus</code> (<code>addAction</code> /
        <code>addFilter</code> / <code>emit</code>) was <strong>retired
        2026-06-12</strong> (<code>plugin-system-pot-port-2026-06-11</code>
        P-006 / D-003: zero registered consumers, and its invocations bypassed
        dispatch — no audit, no fire-time capability gating). It is gone from
        the loader, SDK, and host; the only surviving reference is a
        throw-only browser stub under <code>libs/papercusp/_retired/</code>.
        The live model is two parts:
      </p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>FROZEN typed lifecycle hooks</strong>
        (<code>PluginHooks</code> on the <code>Plugin</code> interface —
        <code>onLoad</code>, <code>onUnload</code>,
        <code>onHarnessCreated</code>, <code>beforeMissionStart</code>,
        <code>afterDone</code>, <code>onFeaturePassed</code>,
        <code>onPostWorker</code>, etc.). The existing fire-points stay for
        back-compat, but no new ones will be added — new host fire-points
        ship as event emissions instead.</li>
        <li><strong>Capability-scoped event-reaction rules</strong>
        (<code>PluginReactionRule</code>) — the public extension surface. A
        plugin declares <code>reactions: PluginReactionRule[]</code> (code
        form) or manifest <code>reactions</code> (declarative subset); when a
        rule's trigger <code>on</code> settles (a tool invocation observed at
        the dispatcher, or a host emission like
        <code>pipeline:step-done</code>), the host fires the rule's
        <code>fire</code> target through <strong>normal dispatch</strong> —
        auth-gated, quota'd, audited, loop-protected. The
        <code>events:listen:&lt;trigger&gt;</code> /
        <code>events:emit:&lt;name&gt;</code> capabilities still exist, gating
        reaction-rule triggers and plugin event emissions (not a hook bus).</li>
      </ul>

      <p>
        The reaction registry enforces a different namespace rule than the old
        bus: a rule's <code>fire</code> target must be one of the plugin's
        <strong>own</strong> projected tools
        (<code>&lt;plugin&gt;.&lt;verb&gt;</code>) — the host throws if the
        fire target belongs to another plugin. There is no list of reserved
        event prefixes being rejected. The richer ordering / guard / slot
        machinery in §8.5.1–§8.5.5 below (named predicates, integer priority,
        <code>addGuard</code>/<code>VETO</code>,
        <code>useSlot</code>/<code>declareAction</code>) is design intent and
        is <strong>not</strong> in the shipped SDK.
      </p>

      <p>
        Plugins extend behaviour without modifying core, via named hooks:
      </p>

      

```
// Plugin code:
api.hooks.addAction('task.passed', async (task) => {
  // Generate a briefing video when the milestone task passes
  await generateBriefingVideo(task);
});

api.hooks.addFilter('task.title', (title, task) => {
  // Prepend a tag to every task title
  return '[briefings] ' + title;
});

// Substrate fires:
await api.hooks.runAction('task.passed', task);
const finalTitle = await api.hooks.applyFilter('task.title', task.title, task);
```



      <p>
        Hook names (and their argument shapes) are part of the spec. Plugins declare `events:listen:&lt;name&gt;` capabilities to subscribe.
      </p>

      

### 8.5.1 Hook ordering — named predicates (canonical) + priority (fallback)



      <p>
        When multiple plugins register for the same hook, the substrate
        determines execution order. Two ordering models are supported.
        <strong>Predicates are the canonical form</strong>; integer priorities
        exist as a fallback for ports of WordPress-style code.
      </p>

      <h4>8.5.1.a Named ordering predicates (preferred)</h4>

      <p>
        Authors declare relationships, not absolute numbers. The substrate
        topologically sorts handlers and <strong>caches the resolved order
        per-hook-name</strong>; the sort runs at install/uninstall/update
        time, not on every fire. A hot hook like `task.passed`
        firing thousands of times per minute reads its cached order with
        no per-fire sort overhead.
      </p>

      <p>
        Cache invalidation triggers: any plugin install, uninstall, update,
        or capability change that would alter the handler set for that hook.
        The substrate doesn't expose a manual cache flush — there's no
        scenario where the resolved order changes without one of those
        events.
      </p>

      ```typescript
api.hooks.addAction('task.passed', handler, { runs: 'after:audit-log' });
api.hooks.addAction('task.passed', handler, { runs: 'before:billing' });
api.hooks.addAction('task.passed', handler, { runs: ['after:audit-log', 'before:billing'] });
```

      <p>
        Each predicate is `before:&lt;name&gt;` or
        `after:&lt;name&gt;`, where `&lt;name&gt;` is
        another handler's plugin name or a substrate-defined named anchor
        (e.g. `after:substrate.audit-log`). Multiple predicates
        AND together.
      </p>

      <p>
        Cycles in the dependency graph are <strong>install-time errors</strong>,
        not silent runtime races. References to unknown handlers are warnings
        (handler still registers, predicate is treated as satisfied).
      </p>

      ```
$ papercusp install plugin-x
Error: hook 'task.passed' has a cycle:
  audit-log → billing → audit-log
Two plugins both declare runs:'after:' on each other. Pick a primary owner
and switch the other to runs:'before:'.
Aborted.
```

      <h4>8.5.1.b Integer priorities (fallback)</h4>

      <p>
        For compatibility with WordPress-style code, integer priorities are
        also accepted. Lower numbers run first; default priority is <strong>10</strong>.
      </p>

      ```typescript
api.hooks.addAction('task.passed', handler, { priority: 5 });   // runs first
api.hooks.addAction('task.passed', handler);                    // priority 10 (default)
api.hooks.addAction('task.passed', handler, { priority: 20 });  // runs last
```

      <p>
        Mixed handlers (some predicate, some priority) resolve in two passes:
        the substrate first sorts the predicate-using handlers topologically,
        then interleaves the priority-using handlers at their integer position
        relative to that sorted list. Authors should not mix the two models in
        the same hook chain — the resulting order is well-defined but harder
        to reason about than picking one.
      </p>

      <h4>8.5.1.c Action vs filter semantics</h4>

      <p><strong>Action chains</strong> run for side effects; all handlers fire regardless of return value. <strong>Filter chains</strong> pipe the value through each handler in order; each handler receives the previous handler's output.</p>

      ```typescript
// Two plugins both filter task.title:
// Plugin A: addFilter('task.title', t => '[A] ' + t, { runs: 'after:audit-log' })
// Plugin B: addFilter('task.title', t => '[B] ' + t, { runs: 'after:billing' })
//
// If neither names the other, registration order tiebreaks.
// If A says { runs: 'after:billing' }, B runs first → final = '[A] [B] do thing'
```

      <p><strong>Cancellation.</strong> A filter handler that returns the special papercup `api.hooks.STOP` halts the chain — no further handlers run, the current value is returned. Useful for veto patterns (e.g., a security plugin blocks a task title containing PII). For preventing actions from happening at all, see §8.5.2 (Guard hooks).</p>

      

### 8.5.2 Guard hooks — pre-fact veto



      <p>
        Action and filter hooks run <em>during</em> or <em>after</em> an
        operation. They can observe and (for filters) transform values, but
        they cannot prevent the operation from happening. <strong>Guard hooks</strong>
        run <em>before</em> an operation and can short-circuit it entirely.
      </p>

      ```typescript
// Plugin code — block routine fires that exceed a per-fire cost cap:
api.hooks.addGuard('routine.beforeFire', (routine, ctx) => {
  if (routine.estimated_cost_cents > 5000) {
    return api.hooks.VETO('over per-fire $50 cap');
  }
  // returning nothing = approve
});

// Plugin code — block task creation with PII in title:
api.hooks.addGuard('task.beforeCreate', (task) => {
  if (containsPII(task.title)) {
    return api.hooks.VETO('PII detected in task title');
  }
});
```

      <p>
        When ANY guard returns `VETO`, the operation aborts and
        the substrate surfaces the reason to whoever initiated it (the
        orchestrator, a routine fire, the user UI). Guard hooks run with
        the same predicate-ordering semantics as actions; if multiple guards
        veto, all reasons are surfaced together.
      </p>

      <p><strong>Naming convention.</strong> Substrate guards are named
      `X.beforeY` (e.g. `task.beforeCreate`,
      `routine.beforeFire`, `plugin.beforeInstall`).
      Plugin-defined guards follow the same pattern.</p>

      <p><strong>Capability gating.</strong> Registering a guard requires
      `events:guard:&lt;hook-name&gt;` in the manifest — separate
      from `events:listen:&lt;hook-name&gt;` for advisory hooks.
      Guards are higher-impact (they can break the substrate's flow), so
      consent prompts surface them prominently.</p>

      

### 8.5.3 Hook namespacing



      <p>
        Substrate-defined hooks live in flat namespaces (`task.passed`,
        `routine.fired`). Plugin-defined hooks <strong>must</strong>
        be prefixed with the plugin name to avoid collisions:
      </p>

      ```typescript
// In plugin "shareholder-briefings" — defines a hook other plugins can listen to:
api.hooks.declareAction('shareholder-briefings.briefingReady', {
  args: { briefing: BriefingSchema },
});

// Other plugins listen with the namespaced name:
api.hooks.addAction('shareholder-briefings.briefingReady', async (args) => {
  await postToSlack(args.briefing);
});
```

      <p>
        The substrate rejects `declareAction()` calls whose hook
        name doesn't begin with the plugin's own name. Listeners can subscribe
        to anything (gated by `events:listen:&lt;hook-name&gt;`),
        but only the owning plugin can fire the hook.
      </p>

      <p>
        This eliminates the WordPress pathology where two unrelated plugins
        each define a `save_post`-shaped hook and step on each other.
      </p>

      

### 8.5.4 Cross-plugin transactions and consistency



      <p>
        Hooks are <strong>post-commit</strong>. When plugin A writes to its
        schema and the substrate fires `plugin-a.rowSaved`, plugin B's
        listener sees the row already committed. If B fails, the substrate
        does <strong>not</strong> roll back A's write.
      </p>

      <p>
        This is eventual-consistency by design. Plugin authors writing
        cross-plugin flows should assume:
      </p>

      <ul>
        <li>The originating write has committed before the hook fires.</li>
        <li>Listener errors are logged to `audit.hook_executions`; subsequent listeners still run.</li>
        <li>Retry logic is the listener's responsibility (e.g. via routines that re-process unsynced rows).</li>
      </ul>

      <p>
        <strong>Saga semantics</strong> (cross-plugin atomicity, compensating
        actions on failure) are out of scope for v1.0. Plugins that need
        transactional cross-plugin behaviour should expose substrate-mediated
        services that wrap the entire flow, rather than relying on hook chains.
      </p>

      

### 8.5.5 Slots — composable surface contributions



      <p>
        §10.5 introduces <code>--supplement</code> as one resolution
        for UI conflicts: a plugin runs as a sibling action when another
        plugin's tab is rendered, "requires papercup to declare it as a
        slot." This section defines what a slot is.
      </p>

      <p>
        A <strong>slot</strong> is a named extension point inside a host
        plugin's UI that other plugins can mount components into. The
        host plugin declares slots in its manifest and renders them with
        a typed component; supplementing plugins target slots by id.
        It's the same pattern as VS Code's "menu contribution points"
        but typed end-to-end.
      </p>

      <p><strong>Host plugin: declare slots.</strong></p>

      ```typescript
// papercup's manifest:
export default defineManifest({
  name: 'papercup',
  ui: {
    slug: 'papercup',
    component: PapercupRoot,
    slots: [
      {
        id: 'directives.row-actions',
        description: 'Per-row action buttons rendered after the default Edit/Delete in the directives table.',
        propsSchema: z.object({
          directive: DirectiveSchema,
          onClose: z.function().returns(z.void()),
        }),
      },
      {
        id: 'briefing-summary.footer',
        description: 'Footer area below the auto-generated briefing summary.',
        propsSchema: z.object({ briefingId: z.string() }),
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

      <p><strong>Host plugin: render the slot.</strong></p>

      ```tsx
// In papercup's React tree:
import { useSlot } from '@papercusp/plugin-sdk/react';


export function DirectivesTableRow({ directive, onClose }) {
  const slotChildren = useSlot('directives.row-actions', { directive, onClose });
  return (
    <tr>
      <td>{directive.title}</td>
      <td>
        <Button onClick={...}>Edit</Button>
        <Button onClick={...}>Delete</Button>
        {slotChildren /* every supplementing plugin's component appears here, in install order */}
      </td>
    </tr>
  );
}
```

      <p><strong>Supplementing plugin: contribute to a slot.</strong></p>

      ```typescript
// shareholder-briefings manifest:
export default defineManifest({
  name: 'shareholder-briefings',
  capabilities: ['ui:slot:papercup:directives.row-actions'],
  ui: {
    slug: 'shareholder-briefings',
    component: BriefingsRoot,
    slotContributions: [
      {
        slot: 'papercup:directives.row-actions',
        component: GenerateBriefingButton,
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

      <p><strong>Substrate guarantees.</strong></p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Typed props.</strong> The host's <code>propsSchema</code>
        is the contract. Supplementing components receive props validated
        against that schema; a mismatch is an install-time error.</li>
        <li><strong>Capability gating.</strong> Slot contributions require
        the resource-shaped capability
        <code>ui:slot:&lt;owner&gt;:&lt;slot-id&gt;</code>. Users
        consent at install time per slot, not blanket.</li>
        <li><strong>Failure isolation.</strong> A supplementing component
        crash is caught by an error boundary the substrate wraps around
        each slot child. The host's render tree continues; the broken
        contribution shows a 1-line "X failed to render — see logs"
        placeholder.</li>
        <li><strong>Order.</strong> Within a slot, contributions render
        in install order by default. A contribution can declare a
        `position` field of `'first'`, `'last'`, `{ before: 'plugin-name' }`,
        or `{ after: 'plugin-name' }` — same predicate model as hook
        ordering (§8.5.1.a).</li>
        <li><strong>Slot deprecation.</strong> Removing or renaming a
        slot is a major-version event for the host plugin, just like
        a service ABI break (§8.4.1). Substrate refuses load when
        a contribution targets a removed slot.</li>
        <li><strong>Adding a new slot is additive</strong> (§8.4.1) — a minor
        version bump for the host plugin. Existing supplementing plugins
        keep working; new contributors can target the new slot. Renaming
        the slot's <code>propsSchema</code> to be <em>more</em> permissive
        (e.g., adding optional fields) is also additive; tightening the
        schema (e.g., adding a required field, narrowing a union) is a
        major-version event because existing contributors break.</li>
      </ul>

      <p><strong>Plugin-defined slots prefix.</strong> Like hook names
      (§8.5.3), slot ids declared inside a plugin must be referenced as
      <code>&lt;owner&gt;:&lt;slot-id&gt;</code> from outside. This
      keeps two unrelated plugins from accidentally claiming the same
      slot id.</p>

      

### 8.6 v2 sandboxing — iframe + postMessage RPC



      <p>
        When the marketplace ships, plugins load as iframes:
      </p>

      

```
<!-- Host renders for each registered plugin: -->
<iframe
  src="https://plugin-cdn.papercusp.com/<name>/<version>/index.html"
  sandbox="allow-scripts"
  csp="default-src 'self'; connect-src https://youtube.com https://googleapis.com"
/>

<!-- Inside the iframe: -->
<script>
  import { connectHostApi } from '@papercusp/plugin-sdk/iframe';
  const api = await connectHostApi();   // postMessage RPC handshake
  // Now `api` works just like the v1 in-process version
</script>
```



      <p>
        Same plugin code, same DI calls — only the loader changes. CSP enforces network allowlist; iframe sandbox enforces no DOM/storage access outside the plugin.
      </p>

      <p>
        <em>Implemented (current state):</em> the
        <code>@papercusp/plugin-sdk/iframe</code> subpath has shipped, but the
        v2 sandbox model above is still design intent. The live iframe-bridge
        surface is <code>initPapercupIframe()</code> plus the
        <code>usePapercupAction</code> / <code>usePapercupEvent</code> /
        <code>usePapercupQuery</code> helpers (not a single
        <code>connectHostApi()</code> handshake as sketched here).
      </p>

      

### 8.7 Two distribution channels: tarball-install vs iframe-CDN



      <p>
        The marketplace described in §11 ships <strong>tarballs</strong> that get installed locally and run in-process with the substrate. The iframe model in §8.6 describes a different channel — <strong>CDN-hosted iframe widgets</strong>. Both will exist; they target different use cases:
      </p>

      <table>
        <thead>
          <tr><th>Channel</th><th>Use case</th><th>Code lives</th><th>Capability boundary</th><th>Trust model</th></tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Tarball install</strong> (primary)</td>
            <td>Full plugins: roles, schemas, routines, API routes, full-route UI panels. Anything that needs Postgres or long-lived state.</td>
            <td>`~/.papercusp/installed/&lt;name&gt;/` after `papercusp install`</td>
            <td>Function-call DI proxy (in-process)</td>
            <td>User-grants capabilities at install time; plugin runs with full DI access for granted caps. Capability scope is the security perimeter.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Iframe widget</strong> (v2, supplementary)</td>
            <td>Embeds, charts, demos, third-party visualizations, anything ephemeral that doesn't need substrate state. Also: untrusted plugins where the user wants stronger isolation.</td>
            <td>CDN bundle at `https://plugin-cdn.papercusp.com/&lt;name&gt;/&lt;version&gt;/`</td>
            <td>iframe sandbox + CSP + postMessage RPC</td>
            <td>User picks per-plugin trust level. Iframe defaults to no DI access; capabilities only granted via postMessage RPC after explicit user approval.</td>
          </tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

      <p>
        A given plugin can ship as <em>either</em>. A few that do both: `weather-widget` ships as an iframe (just a chart), `shareholder-briefings` ships as a tarball (registers a routine + a role + a schema). A plugin that wants both forms publishes two manifests with the same name (CLI handles it; the user picks at install time).
      </p>

      <p><strong>Important caveat:</strong> the iframe sandbox stops DOM access and unlisted network calls. It does <em>not</em> add isolation for the DI surface — if the iframe is granted `db:plugin-schema`, it can still issue queries through the postMessage proxy. The DB write can hit the same Postgres rows as a tarball plugin's write. <strong>The iframe boundary is a network/DOM boundary, not a data boundary.</strong> If you need true data isolation, run the substrate against a separate database namespace (see §10.5).</p>

      <p><strong>Latency caveat.</strong> Every DI call from inside an iframe
      is a postMessage RPC round-trip — typically 1–5ms. Per-frame interactions
      (timeline scrubbers, drag handles, scroll-driven charts, audio
      visualizers, anything inside a 16ms render budget) cannot afford that.
      <strong>Iframe widgets are appropriate for read-mostly or
      ephemeral surfaces; use a tarball install for any UI that touches the
      DI surface in a render loop.</strong> Authors who attempt high-frequency
      iframe RPC will hit jank that no engineering inside the plugin can fix.</p>

### 8.8 Iframe-host routes inside the operator app

<p>A dashboard tab (<code>dashboardTabs[]</code> entry) can ship as an
<strong>in-process React component</strong> (<code>componentRoot</code> +
<code>componentId</code>) or an <strong>iframe</strong>
(<code>iframeUrl</code>, or <code>iframeUrlConfigKey</code> resolved against
the plugin's config). When both are present, the host prefers the iframe URL
(cheaper to validate at runtime; no rebuild required to update). An
iframe-mode tab can point at any URL — a separate origin like
<code>localhost:8082</code> for code-server, or a route on the operator
itself. The latter is the <strong>iframe-host route</strong> pattern: the
plugin contributes nothing but a manifest, and the operator app renders the
actual UI at a dedicated route. <code>@papercupai/starlight</code> follows
this shape today (it is the successor to the outgoing
<code>@papercupai/fumadocs</code> — fumadocs the framework was migrated to
Astro Starlight): its tab declares
<code>iframeUrlConfigKey: "docsUrl"</code>, defaulting to
<code>http://localhost:3055/project-docs</code>.
(<code>@papercupai/pi-coding</code> originally used this pattern pointing at
<code>/pi</code>, but has since moved to an inline React dock —
<code>componentRoot</code>/<code>componentId</code> with
<code>embedMode: "inline-dock"</code> — rather than an iframe.)</p>

<p>Two non-obvious requirements when adding such a route:</p>

<ol>
  <li><strong>Replicate provider context.</strong> The route inherits only the
      app's root layout. Components that "just work" inside
      <code>/harness/*</code> may rely on harness-scoped providers (for example
      <code>Tooltip.Provider</code>, <code>HarnessSyncProvider</code>) that the
      root layout doesn't supply, throwing
      <code>"Tooltip must be used within TooltipProvider"</code> at render.
      Replicate just the providers the embedded component actually uses.</li>
  <li><strong>Strip the global chrome.</strong> The operator's root layout
      always renders the top nav, OracleDock, and Chatwoot widget. Inside an
      iframe-tab those are noise. Drop in
      <code>{'<Chromeless />'}</code> from <code>app/_components/Chromeless.tsx</code>:
      it adds the <code>papercusp-chromeless</code> body class, which
      <code>globals.css</code> uses to hide
      <code>.pc-header</code>, <code>#chatwoot_live_chat_widget</code>, and
      the OracleDock (via its <code>.oracle-dock</code> /
      <code>.oracle-fab</code> class selectors — not the
      <code>data-oracle-dock</code> attribute). Pass <code>auto</code> when the route
      is <em>also</em> meaningful standalone (e.g. <code>/project-docs</code>,
      where direct visitors should still see chrome) — it will only apply
      chromeless when <code>window.self !== window.top</code>.</li>
</ol>

<p>Whether plugin dashboard tabs render <em>at all</em> is gated by the
<code>PAPERCUSP_TABS_FROM_PLUGINS</code> feature flag (the "P7 plugin-tab
cutover", set to <code>1</code> on the substrate process). Given that flag,
the manifest's <code>replaces: ['&lt;built-in-id&gt;']</code> array handles
suppression: the dashboard hides the built-in hard-coded tab (e.g.
<code>docs</code>) when a plugin replacement is present and active. So the two
concerns are distinct — the flag controls whether plugin tabs appear, and
<code>replaces</code> controls which built-in tab the new one supersedes. See
<a href="/docs/implementation/pi-integration">pi integration</a> for the
worked example.</p>
